pages:
Afternoons at {house} belong to rehearsal. The lanterns are unlit, the musicians are in their shirtsleeves, and {first} is on the stage in the middle of the lily pond, running the same eight bars for the twentieth time. Her silver anklets chime on every landing. She says she likes an audience, even an audience of one who is supposed to be doing the accounts.

You are, in fact, doing the accounts. You are just doing them at a table by the stage.

pages.text:
The flute stops first, and the harp a moment after. All four musicians have got to their feet, and the drummer is trying to do up his collar with one hand.

{first} lands a turn, looks past you toward the garden gate, and goes pale to the tips of her ears.

"Don't turn around quickly," she whispers. "That is Lady Silverbough. She paid for this stage. She paid for the pond. She hasn't set foot in here since before I was born."

pavilion.hint: The Pavilion's patroness wants to meet the new owner.
pavilion.text: Lady Ilyana Silverbough, the Pavilion's elven patroness for a century, glides in unannounced. "So. A human bought my garden." She studies you like an unusual insect. "Impress me."

talk.label: Make conversation
talk.win: "Hm. You listen more than you talk. That's rare in humans." She leaves you a pressed moon-lily.
talk.lose: "Hm," she says, and leaves. Not a good "hm."

dance.label: Let {resident} dance for her
dance.win: Ilyana watches without blinking. At the end she says only: "Again, next season."
dance.lose: A stumble. Ilyana says nothing, which is worse.

pages:
The new season opens in three days, and {first} has decided the second-act leap isn't high enough. Nobody else can see anything wrong with it. The musicians have told her so. You have told her so.

She does it again anyway. She has done it forty times since breakfast. You have been counting, because the alternative is doing the accounts. She runs, she jumps, she hangs in the air a moment longer than seems fair, and she lands on the wet boards with her silver-white hair settling after her.

The forty-first time, she comes down a hand's width too close to the edge of the stage. You hear it before you understand it. It's a small sound, like a knuckle cracking.

She doesn't cry out. She sits down very carefully on the boards with her leg out in front of her, and she looks at her ankle as if it has let her down in public.
pavilion.text: "It's only twisted," {resident} says, before you can ask. She tries to stand and can't. The premiere is in three days.

postpone.label: Postpone and let her rest
postpone.res: The premiere slips a week. She heals fully, and she doesn't forget that you chose her over the schedule.

dance.label: Ask her to dance through it
dance.res: She does. Perfectly. She doesn't look at you once afterward.

massage.label: Massage the ankle yourself
massage.lead: Old skills settle right into your hands. By the time the knot eases from her ankle, {resident} isn't letting your wrist go—tugging you onto the rehearsal cushions with flushed cheeks.
massage.situation: In the rehearsal hall after evening practice, Sylphine draws Sam down beside her.
massage.skilled: Old skills. It's good as new by morning, and she's looking at you differently.
massage.unskilled: You have no idea what you're doing. She appreciates the effort anyway.

pages:
The card arrives on a silver tray, because the messenger wouldn't hand it to anyone directly. It is thick cream paper with a single line of very small handwriting on it. {first} reads it standing up. Then she sits down.

"Maestro Valois," she says. "He's coming to the opening."

You tell her that sounds like good news. She gives you the look she gives clients who clap in the wrong place.

pages.text:
"He reviewed the Summer Court's ballet in four words and the company disbanded," she says. "He called my old teacher 'competent' and she retired to grow turnips. He has not written a kind sentence since before the last war, and people in three kingdoms read him over breakfast."

She has been at the barre since then. The cook has sent up six meals and got back six full trays. Tonight the front row has one reserved chair, and a thin elf with a monocle is walking toward it.

pavilion.text:
Maestro Valois, the most feared critic in three kingdoms, takes his seat without a word to anyone and uncaps his pen.

Backstage, {resident} has both hands pressed flat to her stomach. The musicians are all looking at you.

premiere.label: {resident} dances the premiere
premiere.win: Valois's review is one word long: "Transcendent." Half the city tries to book a table.
premiere.lose: Valois writes "Promising." It's devastating. They'll try again next season.

pages:
Lady Ilyana has been in the same seat every night since the review. It is the third table from the pond, facing the stage, with one glass of pale wine that she never finishes. She doesn't applaud. When the last dance ends she rises, inclines her head exactly once toward the stage, and leaves a single moon-lily on the table.

{first} keeps every one of them. There is a row of little glass jars along her windowsill now, and she tops up the water every morning.

pages.text:
Tonight the third table is empty. {first} notices in the middle of a turn, and you can see it cost her a beat. She dances the rest of the set beautifully and comes off the stage frowning.

"She has never missed one," she says. "Not one. Do you think she's ill? Elves don't get ill. Do you think we bored her?"

Behind her, somebody is coming through the garden gate alone. There are tiny pearls in her silver hair, and for once nobody is carrying her things.

pavilion.hint: The patroness has made a decision.
pavilion.text: Ilyana arrives with no entourage and one small bag. "I have owned this garden for a hundred years and never once been part of it. I find I would rather be part of it." She sets down the bag. "I'll want a room with a view of the lilies."

welcome.label: Welcome her home
welcome.res: With Ilyana hosting, the Pavilion draws more refined guests than ever (+15% clients).

pages:
There are buds on the moon-lilies. {first} finds them first and drags you out to the pond in the morning to look. They are tight green spears, hundreds of them, all leaning the same way.

"They open for one night," she says. "All together, at moonrise, and they glow. You can read by it. The whole Elven Quarter comes out into the streets and dances until they close again." She is bouncing on her toes. "I've danced it in the square every year since I was a girl. I have never danced it on a stage."

pages.text:
Ilyana joins you at the pond with a cup of tea. She looks at the buds for some time.

"Nine days," she says. "For a hundred years the festival has gone around this garden. The quarter dances in the lanes and looks at my wall. I thought that was dignified." She sips. "I now think it was merely rude."

pavilion.text: Ilyana sets her cup down. "Open the gate this year," she says. "Let the quarter dance in here, under the lanterns, with {resident} on the stage. It will cost you. I think it is worth it."

sponsor.label: Sponsor the festival
sponsor.res: The Pavilion glows all night. Every dancer's popularity climbs.

pages:
The Underdistrict has no sky, so the night at {house} starts when {first} says it does. She walks the floor at opening with a velvet rope looped over one arm, counting heads and remembering faces. Her heart-tipped tail flicks whenever she passes someone who owes her a favour.

She has been teaching you the room. The corner booth pays in advance. That table cheats at cards. You must never, ever seat an imp near the candles.

pages.text:
Tonight she is halfway through explaining the imp when the room goes quiet. It doesn't happen all at once. It starts at the door and moves inward, table by table, and the people going quiet are the demons. The humans keep talking for a few seconds longer, until they notice.

{first}'s tail has stopped moving. It is the first time you have ever seen it still.

"Don't stand up," she says softly. "Don't offer her a drink. And whatever she calls you, don't answer to it."

veil.hint: The Underdistrict's landlord has noticed you.
veil.text:
A four-horned demoness drapes herself across the bar. "Vharra. I own the Underdistrict, darling. Including the ground under your little den. Rent is tripling."

{resident} hisses at her.

pay.label: Pay her off
pay.res: "Good boy." She'll want more later. She always does.

flirt.label: Flirt back
flirt.win: Vharra blinks, then laughs. "Oh, you're FUN." Rent stays the same. For now.
flirt.lose: She pats your cheek. "Adorable. Rent is due next week."

refuse.label: Refuse
refuse.win: Vharra looks around at your security, then at you, and smiles slowly. "Interesting."
refuse.lose: Vharra laughs and leaves. She'll be back.

pages:
It's a slow night at {house}, and you make the mistake of saying so out loud. You are leaning on the end of the bar watching {first} work the floor. She greets a table, tops up a glass, turns a quarrel into a joke, and steers a drunk toward the door with two fingers on his elbow. From where you stand it looks like a pleasant walk.

"It doesn't seem that hard," you say to the bartender.

The bartender takes a step away from you.

{first} is on the far side of the room, with a band playing between you. She turns her head anyway. Demons have very good ears. She crosses the floor without hurrying, and her gold eyes don't leave your face, and her smile gets wider with every step.
veil.hint: Zaria has a wager in mind.
veil.text: {resident} bets you can't survive one night working the Veil's floor yourself: greeting, pouring, keeping the peace, the works.

bet.label: Take the bet
bet.lead: You survive. Barely. {resident} tosses a pouch of 150g onto the bar, then locks the back parlor door and pushes you onto the velvet settee. "Winner's privilege, darling. I collect in person."
bet.situation: After hours behind the Veil, Zaria settles a wager privately with Sam.
bet.win: You survive. Barely. Zaria pays up, impressed: +150g.
bet.lose: You last until midnight. Zaria collects her winnings—your pride—and kisses your cheek.

pages:
The first night it's a broken glass, and you think nothing of it. The second night it's a chair. On the third night two strangers start a fight over a card game that neither of them was playing, and four regulars leave without finishing their drinks.

The faces are different every night. {first} clears up after each of them with a smile that has stopped reaching her eyes. Then she brings you the till.

"Look at the coin," she says, and tips a handful onto your desk.

It takes you a moment. Every troublemaker this week paid for his first drink before he started breaking things, and they all paid in the same money. They're old Underdistrict pieces with a ring of green wax pressed into the rim, and each one is stamped with four small horns.
veil.hint: Vharra is not done with you.
veil.text: "Vharra's tenants," {resident} says. Her tail is lashing. "She's testing us. She wants to see whether we pay, or break, or beg. They'll be back tonight."

hold.label: Hold the line
hold.win: Night after night, the Veil throws them out. Eventually, they stop coming.
hold.lose: It's a bad week. The Veil needs better security.

pages:
It has been a quiet week. Nothing has been broken. Nobody has paid in green-stamped coin. {first} doesn't trust it at all, and she has doubled the watch on the door.

"She's lost before," she says. "She has never once lost quietly. In three hundred years I have seen her burn down a bakery over a late pie." She thinks about that. "It was a very good bakery."

pages.text:
So when Vharra comes down the stairs tonight, the whole room braces. She has come alone. Nobody is walking ahead of her and there's no collector at her shoulder. The gold rings on her four horns catch the lamplight.

She orders a drink at the bar like anybody else, and she pays for it, in ordinary coin. {first} watches her count out the change with open suspicion.

Then she picks up her glass and walks straight to your table.

veil.text: Vharra sits down across from you, uninvited. "Fine. You win. Do you know how boring it is, collecting rent for three hundred years?" She leans in. "I'd rather MAKE money. Here. With you. And I'll cut your rent, obviously."

hire.label: Hire her
hire.res:
Vharra joins the Veil, and its upkeep drops by 30%.

{resident} rolls her eyes, but she's grinning. "Fine. And you can keep my wages, Zaria's rules. Try not to bore me, Sam."

pages:
Putting Vharra and {first} under one roof has gone about as you expected. They are both too professional to fight in front of clients. They snipe instead. They do it across the floor, in passing, in a demon dialect you don't speak, and both of them are smiling the whole time.

You have asked each of them what the other did. Vharra says it was two hundred years ago and she was entirely in the right. {first} says it was two hundred and six years ago, and that she was.

Tonight, after closing, you find them at the corner booth with a single candle between them. Neither is speaking. {first} has a deck of cards in front of her. It is old and soft at the edges, and the backs are painted with little crimson flowers.

"One game," she says, without looking up. "Winner was right. Loser never mentions it again." She pushes the deck across the table toward the empty third seat. "We agreed on exactly one thing, darling. Neither of us trusts the other to shuffle."
veil.hint: Vharra and Zaria have unfinished business.
veil.text: You sit down in the third seat and pick up the deck. Two demons with two hundred years of grudge between them watch your hands.

deal.label: Deal fairly and keep the peace
deal.win: A draw, somehow. They shake hands. The whole Veil exhales. (Staff mood way up.)
deal.lose: Zaria loses. She sulks for a week. But the feud is over.

cheat.label: Cheat for Zaria
cheat.res: Zaria wins. Vharra absolutely knows, and respects it.

pages:
{first} keeps a tally book for the stable as well as the rooms. Every evening she walks the yard with the pencil from behind her ear and counts wagons. She says an inn at a crossroads lives on wheels, and that the beds are only where the wheels sleep.

This week the count is wrong. The Halbrecht salt train is four days late. The wool factors from the east came in with half their wagons and wouldn't say where the rest were. Six stalls are standing empty, and they are never empty at this time of year.

Tonight a man walks into the yard on foot. He's a carter. You can tell by his hands, and by the way he looks around for a team that isn't there. He has one boot, and a cut over his eye that somebody has stitched badly.

{first} has him in a chair by the hearth with a bowl of soup before he has finished saying his name. She listens to the whole story. Then she comes over to you, wiping her hands on her apron, and for once she isn't smiling.
wayfarer.text: "Red Oskar's gang," {resident} says. "Bandits, on the east road. They took his wagon, his team and one of his boots. If the merchants stop coming, Sam, we're finished."

guards.label: Hire caravan guards
guards.res: The next three caravans arrive safely. Oskar will not be pleased.

ride.label: Ride out with a caravan
ride.win: The bandits take one look at the caravan, decide it isn't worth it, and leave. You pretend that was the plan.
ride.lose: The caravan is robbed. You come back with nothing but a sunburn.

pages:
It has rained since noon, and the common room is full of steaming cloaks. {first} is at the front desk doing what she does with every arrival, which is reading them. She has explained it to you: you look at the boots first, the hat second, and the face last, because faces lie.

"Grain merchant, two nights, will haggle," she murmurs as the door opens. "Pilgrim. He's got no money, so give him the loft." The door opens again, and she stops.

The woman in the doorway wears a plain grey travelling cloak with the hood up, and it is soaked through. She carries her own bag. She has come in from the stable side, which means she arrived on horseback and saw to the horse herself.

{first} leans toward you without taking her eyes off her.

"That cloak cost eight silver," she says under her breath. "Those boots cost forty gold, and they have never been walked in. I don't know what she is, Sam. I always know."
wayfarer.text: The cloaked woman asks {resident} for a room and "absolute discretion." She puts a coin on the desk before anyone has told her the price.

room.label: Give her the best room, on the house
room.res: She thanks you quietly and leaves before dawn. Bettina has a feeling about this.

pages:
The east road is quieter, but nobody thinks it's over. Red Oskar's men have only moved further out. A tinker saw campfires from the ridge. A drover lost two mules and counted himself lucky.

"A gang that size has to eat," {first} says. She is rolling out pastry on the kitchen table as she says it, and she is hitting it rather hard. "It has to drink, and it has to get its horses shod. Somebody sells them flour. Somebody else buys what they steal. And every one of those somebodies sleeps under a roof on the way."

She wipes the flour off her hands and opens the tally book. She doesn't turn to the stable pages or the rooms. She turns to the back, where the columns have no headings.

There are names in it. There are dates, and what each traveller ate, and what they complained about, and what they let slip over their second ale. It goes back ten years.

"I never meant it for anything," she says, a little embarrassed. "I just like to know who's under my roof."
wayfarer.text: "Every traveler talks to the innkeeper," {resident} says. "Give me a few days and I'll find out where Oskar sleeps."

network.label: Let {resident} work her network
network.win: Three days and a lot of free pie later: an old mill, two hours east.
network.lose: The trail goes cold. For now.

money.label: Follow the money
money.win: Stolen goods have to be sold somewhere. You trace them to a fence, and the fence to an old mill.

pages:
The old mill stands two hours east of the Crossroads, at the end of a cart track that the forest has mostly taken back. You leave before dawn. {first} packs you a satchel of food as if you were going on a picnic, then stands in the yard with her arms folded and watches you out of sight.

The wheel fell in years ago. But there is smoke coming from the chimney, and fresh ruts in the track. A wagon is standing behind the building with the Halbrecht salt mark still on its side.

pages.text:
Nobody stops you on the way in. That worries you more than a sentry would have.

Inside there are a dozen men around a fire, eating somebody else's cheese. They look up one after another. The big one at the far end, with the red beard and the eyepatch, doesn't bother to stand. He finishes chewing first.

wayfarer.hint: Time to deal with Red Oskar.
wayfarer.text: The old mill. Red Oskar looks you up and down. "The innkeeper's boy. You've got guts, I'll give you that."

storm.label: Storm the mill
storm.win:
Oskar's gang scatters. The east road is safe, and merchants flood back (+30% merchant clients).

{resident} hugs you so hard you squeak. "No more wages. You saved this inn."

work.label: Offer him honest work
work.win:
Oskar laughs, then thinks about it. A month later he's guarding caravans for good money, and merchants flood back (+30% merchant clients).

{resident} shakes her head in disbelief. "No more wages. You saved this inn."
work.lose: Oskar isn't ready to go straight. Yet.

pages:
There is not an empty stall at {house}. Wagons are parked two deep in the lane, and {first} has started renting out space in the hayloft and feeling guilty about how much she charges for it. She has worn her pencil down to a stub and started a second tally book.

Yesterday a man spent the whole afternoon in the yard with a measuring chain. He paced out the stable. He counted the troughs, and he looked down the well. When {first} asked him his business he bowed and said that he was not at liberty to say.

Today he is back, and this time he brings a clerk, a folding desk and a wax seal the size of a plum. He sets the desk up in the middle of the common room. The seal is the Merchant Guild's. You can tell because every merchant in the room has stopped eating to stare at it.

{first} appears at your elbow. She has taken off her apron and put the pencil back behind her ear.

"Whatever he offers," she whispers, "ask for the stabling fees on top."
wayfarer.text: The merchant guild offers the Wayfarer an exclusive charter: every guild caravan stops here first.

accept.label: Accept (the guildmaster's wife insists it's free)
accept.res: The cloaked traveler was the guildmaster's wife. The charter is free: +60g every week.

buy.label: Buy the charter
buy.res: The guild caravans arrive like clockwork: +60g every week.

pages:
Mornings at {house} begin with a bell and end with a queue. The Quiet Chapel sits at the heart of the cloister, and pilgrims start lining up along the sunlit colonnade before the dew is off the flagstones. They come in worried and go out looking ten years younger. Most of them leave something in the offering box.

{first} takes each of them by the hands at the chapel door. Her halo brightens a little every time. She says she can't help that, and you don't believe her.

Today there's a man in the queue who isn't a pilgrim. He wears cathedral grey and has a satchel with a seal on the flap, and he stands very straight so as not to touch anybody. When he reaches the front he doesn't offer his hands. He offers a rolled parchment, at arm's length, as though it might be catching.

{first} thanks him warmly and wishes him a restful day. He leaves at something close to a run. She breaks the seal with her thumbnail, reads it once, and then walks to the lectern, still reading.
sanctuary.hint: A cathedral inspector wants to shut the Cloister down.
sanctuary.text: {resident} sets a parchment writ from the High Cathedral across the lectern. "They say a Quiet Chapel shouldn't smell of wine and warm sheets. An auditor comes at month's end to revoke our blessing."

precedent.label: Find old precedent in the canon
precedent.win: Tucked behind three centuries of tax rolls, an ancient charter explicitly protects "hospices of lantern and mercy." Caelia grins wide enough to show teeth.
precedent.lose: The church archive clerks stonewall you until dusk.

donate.label: Donate to the cathedral restoration fund
donate.res: Gold smooths a dozen wrinkled brows. The audit turns polite—at least on paper.

pages:
The last pilgrim goes home a little after the evening bell. You are walking the chapel with the long brass snuffer, putting out candles row by row. It has become your job because you are the only one tall enough who doesn't have wings to get in the way.

{first} has heard forty confessions today. You counted the queue. She is sitting inside the velvet confessional with the curtain open and her shoes off, rubbing the arch of one foot, with her gold-tipped feathers drooping over the armrest.

"Forty," she says. "Do you know what people confess to an angel, Sam? Hardly ever the big things. They tell me they were short with their mother. They looked at the baker's wife. They wished the neighbour's dog would die, and then it did." She laughs, tiredly. "Everybody in this quarter gets to put it down somewhere."

She looks at you over the snuffer. The teasing has gone out of her face, and what's left is kinder and a good deal harder to meet.
sanctuary.hint: Caelia has a late confession for you.
sanctuary.text: After bells fade, {resident} pats the seat beside her inside the velvet confessional. "You spend every week listening to everyone else's troubles, Sam. Tell the priestess one selfish wish."

night-off.label: Wish for her to take a night off
night-off.res: Her wings flutter lightly against the wood screen. "Greedy boy," she whispers—and smiles all week.

truth.label: Tell her the truth of what you want
truth.lead: Caelia shuts the velvet curtain behind you, halo burning warm gold in the tight space as she slides straight into your lap. "Then take your penance, Sam."
truth.situation: Inside the velvet confessional after bells, Caelia closes the curtain with Sam.
truth.res: "Already sitting beside me," Caelia purrs, grazing your knuckles with bright halo-warm fingers.

pages:
The sermon was preached on Sunday at Saint Aurel's, two parishes over. You weren't there, but you have had it repeated to you eleven times. The priest named {house} from the pulpit. He described at length what he had heard goes on in the Quiet Chapel, with gestures. He warned his flock that a man might walk in there with a heavy conscience and come out again whistling.

It seems his flock paid close attention.

By Tuesday the queue runs out of the colonnade, across the courtyard and through the gate. There are people in it you have never seen before. Some have come in carriages. One woman has brought a folding stool and her knitting.

{first} looks out at them through the chapel door with her hand over her mouth. Her shoulders are shaking. It takes you a moment to work out that she is trying very hard not to laugh in a holy place.
sanctuary.hint: The quarter is whispering about Caelia.
sanctuary.text: Word has spread faster than prayer: pilgrims line the courtyard at dusk asking specifically for {resident}'s "gentle penance." Half the neighborhood thinks it's scandalous. The other half wants reservations.

mystique.label: Turn scandal into mystique
mystique.win: You rebrand the evening vigil with velvet ropes and lantern oil. Donations double overnight.
mystique.lose: A clumsy flyer leaves the clergy bristling. You try again next week.

pages:
It's the last day of the month. You have been up since before the bell. You have dusted the lectern twice. The paper that answers the cathedral's writ is in the lectern drawer, and you have checked that it is still there more often than you would like to admit.

{first} is not nervous at all, which makes it worse. She has spent the afternoon hearing pilgrims as usual. When you ask whether the Cloister should perhaps be a little less itself tonight, she pats your cheek.

"If he's coming to see what we are," she says, "then let him see it."

So the dusk service goes ahead. The chapel is warm and gold and smells of beeswax. Six merchants from the cloth exchange are kneeling along the front rail, where they have been for the best part of an hour, and not one of them has looked at his pocket watch.

The door at the back opens on a draught of cold air. You see a grey cassock, a silver chain, and a face already arranged to disapprove.
sanctuary.hint: The bishop arrives for an audit.
sanctuary.text: The cathedral envoy arrives unannounced during dusk service, only to freeze at the velvet threshold—watching {resident}'s golden halo glow warm over half a dozen weeping, smiling, remarkably relaxed merchants.

confession.label: Invite the envoy to stay for confession
confession.win:
He leaves two hours later with untied collar strings, a lighter purse, and a signed renewal seal.

{resident} laughs softly against your chest. "No wages needed, Sam. I belong right here."
confession.lose: The envoy clears his throat stiffly and promises a written ruling next week.

pages:
For a week the children of the Lantern Quarter have been leaving things on the Cloister steps. They leave paper lanterns with candle stubs inside, and jam jars with holes punched in the lids, and one very large turnip, hollowed out and carved with a smiling face. Nobody asked them to. {first} says they do it every year, at every door in the quarter where somebody was kind to them.

There are a great many on your steps. She has counted them twice.

You find her sitting among them at sunset with a lapful of late flowers, weaving crowns. She has made eleven. One of them is on her own head, tipped over one eye, and her halo is shining through the petals.

"Candlemas," she says. "The longest night. The whole ward stays awake together until the sun comes up, so nobody has to sit through the dark alone." She holds up a crown, looks at the size of it against your head, and adds another flower. "I have an idea. You're going to say it's too expensive."
sanctuary.hint: The Lantern Quarter holds its Candlemas.
sanctuary.text: "A free vigil," {resident} says. "For the whole ward, here, until sunrise. Food and candles, and nobody turned away." She sets the crown on your head. "Or we keep the velvet rope up and give the regulars a quiet night. You choose."

sponsor.label: Sponsor the Candlemas Vigil
sponsor.res: Hymns and laughter echo down the quarter until dawn. The Cloister's name is spoken with reverence—and fond grins.

velvet.label: Keep the doors velvet-roped for regulars
velvet.res: Exclusive candlelight suites draw steady crowds (+10% clients).

pages:
{first} keeps better books than you do. Her ledger is ruled by hand in lines so straight that they look printed. Every entry is timed to the minute. She notes each client's pulse on the way in and on the way out. There is a column for pillow height.

So when her own earnings come up short, you assume the mistake is yours. You add the week again. Then you add the month. Every week, to the copper, exactly three tenths of what she earns never reaches her purse.

You can't find where it goes. No withdrawal is entered and no debt is listed. The money is in one column and then it isn't in the next. She would never make an error like that, and she is the one who ruled the columns.

It is after midnight when you take the ledger down to the maintenance bay to ask her. The conduits in the walls are humming low. She is standing with her back to you, in front of a brass locker you have never seen open, with her fingertips resting on its door.
atelier.hint: Nadia-6 has a lockbox in her maintenance bay.
atelier.text: "My previous guild installed a loyalty governor," {resident} says, without turning around. Her eyes glow pale cyan in the brass. "Thirty percent of my earnings are still routed to an old contract key. I did not enter it in the ledger because I am not able to."

appraisal.label: Inspect the governor with [Appraisal]
appraisal.res: Appraisal spots a hairline shunt along the clasp—an illegal guild leash left unrecorded for twenty years.

conduit.label: Trace the brass conduit lock
conduit.win: Careful tools lift the brass plate without tripping a single spring. The guild lease is void on its face.
conduit.lose: A hidden detent locks tight before you finish. Next week.

pages:
A silk merchant complains about suite three. He's polite about it. He says that at a certain moment, which he will not describe, something in the wall went 'tink'. It put him off, and he would like it known.

{first} takes this harder than you expected. She has mapped the sound of every pipe in the building. She can tell you which conduit is carrying current by its pitch. By her standards, a 'tink' that she didn't put there herself is a personal failure.

By evening she has the wall panel off in the parlor and her hair pinned up out of the way. There are tools laid out on a cloth beside her in order of size. She has put an oilcan in your left hand and your own pocket watch in your right, and she hasn't told you what either of them is for.

The open vent glows a soft orange. It lights the fine seams along her jaw and the brass filigree at her collarbone, and it is honestly hard to keep your eyes on the watch.
atelier.hint: Nadia wants to fine-tune the parlor acoustics.
atelier.text: "Time the interval between pulses," {resident} says, kneeling at the open vent. "When I tell you, put one drop of oil on the third joint. One drop, Sam, not two."

calibrate.label: Calibrate by ear
calibrate.win: The conduits settle into a warm low thrum that relaxes every room upstairs.
calibrate.lose: A pipe whistles loudly before settling down. Nadia laughs—rare and genuine.

compliment.label: Compliment how she looks in the brass glow
compliment.res: Her cheek panels flush soft rose gold. "Anomaly noted, Sam."

pages:
The first full week's earnings go into {first}'s own purse, all of them. She enters the sum in her ledger and then sits looking at the line for almost a minute, which for her is a very long time.

"I have run the projection," she says. "The guild's key has received a payment every seven days for twenty years. This week it received nothing. There are clerks whose only work is to notice that." Her cyan eyes come up to yours. "I estimate four days."

pages.text:
It takes three days. You are in the lobby when the street door bangs back against the wall hard enough to set the glass chimes ringing.

A man in a guild master's leather apron walks in ahead of two bailiffs. He is waving a bill of sale that has gone brown at the folds. He doesn't look at you. He looks around the room as a man does when he is pricing the furniture, and then he looks at {first} in exactly the same way.

atelier.hint: A guild artificer claims Nadia-6 as property.
atelier.text: "Master Artificer Thackery, Tinker's Guild," he says, to the room in general. He holds the bill of sale up for the bailiffs to see. "Property Number Six belongs in our showroom, not a parlor."

law.label: Counter with artisan charter law
law.win: A registered pleasure-house chassis past year twenty is legally emancipated. The bailiffs shrug and escort the artificer out.
law.lose: Thackery waves a guild stamp you don't have the paperwork to answer yet. He will be back next week.

patent.label: Buy out her old patent
patent.res: Five hundred gold closes the guild ledger permanently. Thackery leaves grumbling.

pages:
The papers come by guild courier in a flat leather wallet, and {first} signs for them herself. The signature is new. She practised it for an hour last night on the back of a supply order, trying different slants.

She reads the first page. She reads it again. You know she took it all in the first time, in less than a second, because that is how she reads. She goes through it a third time anyway, slowly, moving her finger under each line the way people do.

"It says 'the bearer'," she tells you. "It doesn't say 'the unit', and it doesn't say 'Property Six'." She folds the page along its creases and puts it inside her jacket, against the filigree at her collarbone. "I would like you to be present for the next part. I have never done anything only because I wanted to. I should like a witness, in case I get it wrong."

She leads you down to the maintenance bay. The little furnace she uses for soldering is already lit.
atelier.hint: Nadia-6 wants to wipe her old ledger.
atelier.text: The guild crest on {resident}'s choker clicks open in her palm. She drops it into the furnace grate without blinking. "My maintenance costs are mine now," she says softly, stepping close to adjust your collar.

toast.label: Toast to a free Atelier
toast.res: {resident} logs a new line in her private ledger—and waves away every copper of her wages. "You keep it, Sam. I am staying right where I chose."

pages:
Once a year the Artisan Ward closes its streets to carts and opens its workshops to anyone who cares to walk in. There are singing clocks and brass birds. There is a mechanical chess player that everybody knows has a boy inside it. The crowds come from as far away as the coast.

This year the printed guide has a new entry. {first} shows it to you without comment. It reads 'No. 14: The Clockwork Atelier. Private acoustic suites, by arrangement with the proprietress.' She has underlined 'proprietress' in very neat pencil.

By mid-morning there is a small crowd on the pavement. Most of them are guild people, with aprons and loupes and ink on their cuffs. A year ago some of them would have looked at {first} and seen an unpaid invoice. Today they have taken their hats off.

"They are requesting a tour," she says, watching them through the glass. "I have finished the new divan. It is tuned to the room's resonant frequency, and I calculate a strong response." She pauses. "Although they did not ask nicely for twenty years."
atelier.hint: An exhibition of clockwork art comes to Hollowmere.
atelier.text: {resident} turns from the window. "I can open the suites and unveil the divan for all of them. Or the doors stay shut, and it remains something only our patrons have seen. I find that I have a preference. I would still like to hear yours."

showcase.label: Host the Guild Showcase
showcase.res: Merchants and inventors leave fascinated and generous (+12% clients).

private.label: Keep it private for patrons only
private.res: Regulars pack the salon all month.
